newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed, Northrop deal has break-up fee.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed, Northrop deal has break-up fee.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp said Thursday its proposed $11.6 billion merger with Northrop Grumman Corp has a break-up fee of about $200 million.
Chairman Norman Augustine told reporters on a conference call the fee was standard for a merger of this size.
Augustine said the merger was a "combination of two very strong and healthy companies" adding that "our plan for the future is creating the best of the best."

He said the recent addition of British Aerospace Plc to Lockheed's bid for the Joint Strike Fighter aircraft would serve as an example of how Lockheed will not impede global competition. The Joint Strike Fighter is a joint project between the United States and the United Kingdom.
The deal will be neutral to slightly accretive to fiscal 1998 earnings and will become increasingly accretive starting in 1999, Augustine said.
Augustine said the combined companies, which employ about 230,000 workers, do not expect any net job losses since both companies are hiring at the moment.

Northrop Chairman Kent Kresa, who has repeatedly stated his company was not for sale, said the merger talks were Lockheed's idea and began in the second quarter before becoming serious over the past month.
Augustine said the merger was to position Lockheed to be a future leader in the global aerospace industry.
"Merging to become efficient is one fact, but I think we're beyond that stage and now we're building for the future ... it gives us staying power and considerable strength," he said.
The deal took Wall Street off guard.
"These are the two companies in the world that are best known for stealth," Augustine quipped, alluding to Northrop's "Stealth Bomber" and Lockheed's "Stealth Fighter."
